parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State the name of the class (group) of fundamental particles that contains a neutrino.
hints: Hint 1: Think about the two families of fundamental particles - quarks feel the strong force, while the other family contains the electron and neutrino and does not.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the two groups of fundamental particles**
All fundamental particles are either quarks or leptons. Quarks interact via the strong force and make up hadrons. Leptons do not feel the strong force. The electron, muon, tau and their neutrinos are all leptons, so a neutrino belongs to the lepton group.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: A hadron $P$ has a charge of $+1e$, where $e$ is the elementary charge. The hadron $P$ is composed of a down antiquark and only one other quark.
parts.text: Identify a possible flavour for this other quark.
hints: Hint 1: Start from the charge of a down antiquark and work out what charge the second quark must add to reach a total of $+1e$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use quark charges to find the missing flavour**
A down quark has charge $-1/3e$, so a down antiquark has the opposite charge, $+1/3e$.

Step 2: **Find the charge needed**
Let the other quark have charge $q$. Then $$+1/3e + q = +1e$$ so $$q = +2/3e$$. The quarks with charge $+2/3e$ are the up-type quarks: up, charm and top. Any one of these gives the correct total charge.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: State what type of hadron is $P$.
hints: Hint 1: Count the quarks in P - one quark plus one antiquark - and recall which hadron family has exactly this structure.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link quark content to hadron type**
Hadrons made of three quarks are baryons, while hadrons made of one quark and one antiquark are mesons. Here P is made of a down antiquark plus only one other quark, so it is a quark-antiquark pair. That is the definition of a meson.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem:
Nucleus $Q$ undergoes radioactive decay to form nucleus $R$, emitting an antineutrino and another particle $X$, as shown in the decay equation.

$$Q \rightarrow R + X + \bar{\nu}$$
parts.text: State what particle is represented by $X$.
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the antineutrino in the equation - only one type of nuclear decay emits an electron together with an antineutrino.

enrichment.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the antineutrino in the equation - only one type of nuclear decay emits an electron together with an antineutrino.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Compare the nucleon numbers of $Q$ and $R$.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens to the total number of nucleons when a neutron simply changes into a proton inside the nucleus.
parts.proper_answer: equal (nucleon numbers of Q and R are the same)
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See why nucleon number is unchanged**
Beta-minus decay converts one neutron into one proton. The total count of nucleons, neutrons plus protons, stays the same, and the emitted electron and antineutrino are leptons with nucleon number zero. So Q and R have equal nucleon numbers.

walkthrough:
Step 1: **See why nucleon number is unchanged**

parts.label: (c)(iii)

markscheme_points.text: (the charge of) R is greater (than Q)

hints: Hint 1: Apply charge conservation to the decay equation, remembering that X carries negative charge away from the parent nucleus.
parts.proper_answer: charge of R is greater than charge of Q
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply charge conservation**
Total charge must balance: charge of Q = charge of R + charge of X. Since X is a $\beta^{-}$ particle with charge $-1e$, R must have one more unit of positive charge to compensate.

Step 2: **Link to protons**
Inside the nucleus a neutron ($0$) becomes a proton ($+1e$), so the proton number increases by 1. Hence the daughter nucleus R has greater positive charge than the parent Q.
